title: Session-window retention savings sim
summary: Spreadsheet-style simulation that models cost and latency impact of different per-session KV/prefix retention windows (TTL) across bursty client workloads. Includes scenario table, sensitivity checks, and a staged rollout recommendation.
content:
Purpose:
Simulate how varying session-level retention windows (the length of time we keep KV/prefix state keyed to a session id) change cache hit-rate, per-token cost, and cold-start latency for bursty client workloads. Goal is to provide an actionable trade-off matrix for product and runtime teams when choosing default retention policies and offering per-tenant overrides.

Background / motivation:
- We currently operate a KV-prefix cache that stores recent prefixes and decoder KV chunks keyed by (tenant, session_id).
- Default retention is aggressive (30s) to limit memory pressure for multi-tenant pools; engineering has proposed increasing per-session retention for high-value clients or routes to reduce repeated warmups during microburst sessions.
- Existing analyses in optimize/ focused on global hit-rate curves by segment; this sim isolates the temporal dimension: how much do longer session windows reduce repeated warm-starts for the same user session vs. increased memory/unit cost?

Methodology overview (spreadsheet workflow):
1) Synthetic workload generator: sampled from production traces (minute-level anonymized sketch) to produce 100k session traces that vary by session length, inter-request gap, and prefix-reuse probability.
2) Configurable variables (spreadsheet inputs):
   - retention_window: 30s, 2min, 10min, 60min, 24h
   - session_arrival_rate: baseline / +20% / -20%
   - prefix_reuse_prob: 10% / 30% / 60% (probability that a later request in same session reuses a prefix cached earlier)
   - average request tokens: 80 (prompt) + 40 (response) default
   - cost_per_gpu_minute: $2.90 (example; sensitivity range $2.0 - $4.0)
   - warmup_extra_tokens: 50 (tokens incurred when a model recomputes KV for warm-start)
3) For each scenario: simulate session timelines, mark cache hits vs cold-starts given retention_window, accumulate extra tokens and GPU-minutes attributable to recomputes, and compute incremental cost and latency delta.

Key assumptions (editable fields in the sheet):
- A cache hit avoids warm_start_extra_tokens entirely; partial hits (prefix overlap) are modeled as reduced warmup cost (approx 30% of full warmup).
- Memory cost is approximated as additional GPU memory pressure leading to 0.5% throughput reduction per 10k active session-states in a node (conservative).
- Prefetch/batched KV fill technique reduces recompute walltime by 20% when retention_window >= 2min.
- 1M requests baseline = 200k sessions (avg session length 5 requests).

Scenario results (representative table extracted from sheet):
Retention window | Hit-rate | Extra warm tokens avoided /1M reqs | Estimated monthly savings ($) | Median P95 latency delta
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
30s              | 18%     | baseline (0)                     | $0                           | 0ms
2min             | 32%     | 120k                             | $3,800                       | -8ms
10min            | 48%     | 260k                             | $8,200                       | -18ms
60min            | 54%     | 310k                             | $9,700                       | -22ms
24h              | 56%     | 325k                             | $10,150                      | -25ms

Interpretation notes:
- Moving from 30s -> 2min yields the largest marginal gain per memory unit: hit-rate +14pp and ~ $3.8k / month on a 1M request baseline.
- Diminishing returns past 10min: 10min->24h only adds ~8pp hit-rate in our trace set, but memory cost and GC complexity increase.
- P95 latency improvements are modest but meaningful for interactive applications; improved latency is concentrated during microburst events where repeated requests occur within retention window.

Sensitivity analyses included in the sheet (tabs):
- Prefix reuse sensitivity: with prefix_reuse_prob=60% the 2min hit-rate jumps to 45% and monthly savings roughly double.
- Cost sensitivity: if cost_per_gpu_minute increases to $4.0, absolute monthly savings scale linearly (+~40%).
- Session churn: if average session lengths shorten (2 requests), savings shrink by ~60% relative to baseline.
- Memory pressure scenario: simulated increased eviction leading to effective retention reduction by 30% in high-load clusters; this reverses most of the benefit for >60min windows.

Operational impacts and risks:
- Memory amplification: per-session retention multiplies stored KV states; need limiters and a circuit-breaker that caps active session-states per node by tenant tier.
- Complexity of per-tenant defaults: offering 24h retention for enterprise customers requires clear billing signals and possibly separate pools (dedicated capacity).
- GC/eviction churn: longer windows may exacerbate peak-time eviction storms; recommended to stagger TTL expirations with jitter.
- Privacy/compliance: storing session-level KV for longer can surface additional compliance constraints (retention controls, delete-on-demand). Coordinate with security/compliance for default retention policy.

Rollout recommendation (staged):
1) Pilot: enable 2min session window for 5% of traffic on hosted api for customers with no memory pressure (feature flag). Monitor memory_active_states, hit-rate delta, P95 token-latency, and GPU utilization for 2 weeks.
2) Expand: if pilot metrics look good, roll to 25% and add a billing experiment to measure uplift vs cost.
3) Enterprise option: offer a configurable per-tenant retention override (2min / 10min / 60min) behind Dedicated offering or with an explicit pricing add-on.
4) Controls: implement per-node session-state soft caps and jittered TTL; add telemetry metrics: session_state_count, retention_hits_by_window, eviction_reasons.

Action items (spreadsheet checkboxes):
- [ ] Add live trace sample from cohort B (INF-3124) to validate prefix_reuse distribution (owner: Marta)
- [ ] Add memory costing model tied to actual node footprints (owner: SRE team)
- [ ] Implement feature-flagged pilot on canary region + dashboard (owner: platform-engineering)
- [ ] Prepare customer-facing FAQ on retention options and pricing (owner: solutions-engineering)

Open questions for design discussion:
- What should the default retention be for free-tier vs paid-tier? (cost parity target?)
- Do we expose retention as a per-route config, or only per-tenant?
- Should we offer automated adaptive retention (increase retention if session hit-rate exceeds threshold) and bill for the additional memory/time?

Appendix (sheet tabs description):
- "Inputs": editable knobs (retention windows, cost, reuse probs) and distributions
- "Sessions": synthetic timeline generation and per-session event log sample
- "Scenarios": table of resulting hit-rates, token-savings, cost impact per 1M requests
- "Sensitivity": param sweeps (cost, reuse, session length, arrival rate)
- "Ops": telemetry and rollout checklist

Notes on uniqueness of this sim vs previous kw/kv analyses:
- Focuses on per-session temporal retention rather than global cache size allocations or prefetch windows.
- Models the memory vs return curve for retention windows in isolation (so teams can reason specifically about TTL knobs).
- Emphasizes staged operational controls and billing implications for offering retention as a product feature.

If you want: I can expand the sheet with a per-tenant ROI calculator (hard-coded price points) and an A/B experiment template (statistical power calc) in the next revision.
